blocks.content: Somewhere in your system there is a call to another service. A database, a payment gateway, a recommendation microservice, something you do not fully control.
Most of the time that call works fine. But when the downstream service starts failing, the naive thing your code does is keep calling it anyway, over and over, for every incoming request.
That is exactly the wrong move. Repeated calls to a service that is already struggling pile on more load, use up threads and connections, and slow your own service down while it waits for timeouts.
The Circuit Breaker pattern exists to stop that spiral. It watches for failures, and once things look bad enough, it stops calling the failing service at all for a while.
A circuit breaker is a stateful guard around a risky call that fails fast once the call has been failing too often, instead of letting every request wait on a doomed attempt.
1. Why calling a failing service again and again makes things worse
blocks.text: 1. Why calling a failing service again and again makes things worse

blocks.content: Imagine a downstream payment service that has started timing out under load. Each call from your service waits the full timeout, say five seconds, before giving up.
If you have a hundred requests per second hitting that call path, you now have hundreds of threads sitting idle, waiting on a service that was never going to answer in time.
Your own service becomes slow and eventually runs out of connections or threads, even though the actual bug lives somewhere else entirely.
The cascading failure
blocks.text: The cascading failure

blocks.content: This is how one failing service takes down its callers, and then their callers, and so on up the chain. It is called a cascading failure, and it is one of the most common causes of large outages.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512281648-836337273.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart showing how a slow failing downstream service holds threads in the caller, slowing it down and spreading failure further upstream

blocks.content: The fix is to stop trying
blocks.text: The fix is to stop trying

blocks.content: Instead of hoping the next call will succeed, a circuit breaker notices the pattern of failure and short circuits future calls immediately, returning an error or a fallback without even attempting the network call.

["Failing fast frees up threads and connections immediately","It stops adding load to a service that is already struggling","It gives the downstream service room to recover instead of being hit constantly","It gives you a clear, fast error to handle instead of a slow timeout"]

It stops adding load to a service that is already struggling

It gives you a clear, fast error to handle instead of a slow timeout

blocks.content: 2. The three states of a circuit breaker
blocks.text: 2. The three states of a circuit breaker

blocks.content: A circuit breaker is named after an electrical circuit breaker, the switch in your fuse box that trips and cuts power when it detects a dangerous surge.
The software version borrows the same idea and the same three states.

["Closed, the normal state where calls pass through as usual","Open, the tripped state where calls fail immediately without being attempted","Half Open, a cautious in between state where a few test calls are allowed through"]
items: Closed, the normal state where calls pass through as usual
Open, the tripped state where calls fail immediately without being attempted
Half Open, a cautious in between state where a few test calls are allowed through

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783495077890-189258274.png
blocks.alt: State machine diagram showing Closed, Open and Half Open states of a circuit breaker with labeled transitions

blocks.title: Think of it as a switch, not a filter
blocks.content: A circuit breaker does not decide whether an individual request is good or bad. It only tracks whether the underlying call has been succeeding or failing recently, and switches state based on that history.
3. The Closed state, calls go through normally
blocks.text: 3. The Closed state, calls go through normally

blocks.content: Closed is the default and healthy state. Every request that comes in results in a real call to the downstream service.
While in this state, the breaker keeps a running count of recent failures. A timeout, a thrown exception, or an error response from the downstream service all count as a failure.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512283392-122956136.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart of the Closed state showing a request calling the downstream service, a failure count reset on success, and an incremented count on failure while staying below the threshold

blocks.content: Counting failures
blocks.text: Counting failures

blocks.content: Most implementations use either a simple rolling count of the last N calls, or a sliding time window, say the last ten seconds, to decide the current failure rate.
Tripping the breaker
blocks.text: Tripping the breaker

blocks.content: As long as the failure count or failure rate stays under the configured threshold, the breaker stays Closed and nothing changes for the caller.
The moment failures cross that threshold, the breaker trips and moves to Open.
4. The Open state, calls fail fast without even trying
blocks.text: 4. The Open state, calls fail fast without even trying

blocks.content: Once the breaker is Open, it stops calling the downstream service entirely. Every request during this state is rejected immediately, usually with a specific exception or a fallback value.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512284888-900058530.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart of a request arriving while the breaker is Open, showing the call rejected immediately with the downstream service never reached and a fallback returned

blocks.content: Fail fast, not fail slow
blocks.text: Fail fast, not fail slow

blocks.content: This is the whole point of the pattern. Instead of every caller waiting out a timeout against a service that is not answering, they get an instant, predictable failure.
The reset timeout
blocks.text: The reset timeout

blocks.content: The breaker does not stay Open forever. It holds a reset timeout, for example thirty seconds, after which it assumes enough time has passed that the downstream service might have recovered.
Once that timeout elapses, the breaker moves itself to Half Open to check.

blocks.title: Why not just retry immediately
blocks.text: If the breaker allowed calls through right after tripping, it would just recreate the exact overload that caused the failures in the first place. The reset timeout gives the downstream service breathing room.

blocks.content: 5. The Half Open state, a cautious probe to test recovery
blocks.text: 5. The Half Open state, a cautious probe to test recovery

blocks.content: Half Open is a trial period. The breaker allows a small, limited number of calls through to the downstream service, instead of the full normal traffic.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512286385-526917160.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart of the Half Open state showing a limited test call sent after the reset timeout, closing the breaker on success and reopening it on failure

blocks.content: Why not just close it immediately
blocks.text: Why not just close it immediately

blocks.content: Going straight from Open back to Closed would mean throwing the full volume of traffic at a service that may still be recovering, which risks tripping the breaker again right away.
What happens to the test calls
blocks.text: What happens to the test calls

blocks.content: If those test calls succeed, the breaker concludes the downstream service is healthy again and moves back to Closed, resuming normal traffic.
If even one of those test calls fails, the breaker assumes the service has not recovered yet, and it moves straight back to Open, restarting the reset timeout.

blocks.title: Limit concurrent test calls
blocks.content: A common implementation detail is to allow only one or a handful of calls through while Half Open, and reject any others as if the breaker were still Open, until the trial calls resolve.
6. State transition rules, summarized
blocks.text: 6. State transition rules, summarized

blocks.content: Putting the three states together gives us a small, predictable state machine with exactly four transitions.

Test call fails, moves back to Open"]]}

blocks.content: Notice there is no direct path from Closed to Half Open, and no direct path from Open to Closed. Every recovery has to pass through the probing step.
7. Implementing a basic circuit breaker
blocks.text: 7. Implementing a basic circuit breaker

blocks.content: At its core, a circuit breaker is just a small state machine plus a few counters. Let us build one piece at a time.
Step one, the state and counters
blocks.text: Step one, the state and counters

blocks.content: We need to track the current state, a failure count, the timestamp of when the breaker last opened, and configuration for the threshold and reset timeout.

codes.python:
import time


class CircuitBreaker:
    """Tracks failure count and switches between CLOSED and OPEN states."""

    def __init__(self, failure_threshold=5, reset_timeout_ms=30000):
        self.state = "CLOSED"
        self.failure_count = 0
        self.failure_threshold = failure_threshold
        self.reset_timeout_ms = reset_timeout_ms
        self.opened_at = None

    def record_success(self):
        self.failure_count = 0
        self.state = "CLOSED"

    def record_failure(self):
        self.failure_count += 1
        if self.state == "HALF_OPEN" or self.failure_count >= self.failure_threshold:
            self.state = "OPEN"
            self.opened_at = time.time() * 1000
            self.failure_count = 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    breaker = CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=3)

    for i in range(1, 4):
        breaker.record_failure()
        print(f"after failure {i}: state={breaker.state}")

    breaker.record_success()
    print(f"after success: state={breaker.state}")

blocks.content: Step two, deciding whether the reset timeout has elapsed
blocks.text: Step two, deciding whether the reset timeout has elapsed

blocks.content: The breaker needs a way to check whether enough time has passed since it opened, so it can move itself into Half Open.

codes.python:
import time


class CircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, failure_threshold=5, reset_timeout_ms=30000):
        self.state = "CLOSED"
        self.failure_count = 0
        self.failure_threshold = failure_threshold
        self.reset_timeout_ms = reset_timeout_ms
        self.opened_at = None

    def record_success(self):
        self.failure_count = 0
        self.state = "CLOSED"

    def record_failure(self):
        self.failure_count += 1
        if self.state == "HALF_OPEN" or self.failure_count >= self.failure_threshold:
            self.state = "OPEN"
            self.opened_at = time.time() * 1000
            self.failure_count = 0

    def can_attempt(self):
        if self.state == "CLOSED":
            return True
        if self.state == "OPEN":
            elapsed = time.time() * 1000 - self.opened_at
            if elapsed >= self.reset_timeout_ms:
                self.state = "HALF_OPEN"
                return True
            return False
        # HALF_OPEN, allow the probe call
        return True


if __name__ == "__main__":
    breaker = CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=1, reset_timeout_ms=500)

    breaker.record_failure()
    print(f"right after tripping: state={breaker.state} can_attempt={breaker.can_attempt()}")

    time.sleep(0.6)
    allowed = breaker.can_attempt()
    print(f"after reset timeout: can_attempt={allowed} state={breaker.state}")

blocks.title: Keep the state machine tiny
blocks.content: Resist the urge to add extra states. Closed, Open and Half Open cover the pattern completely. Anything else, like separate counters for different error types, can live outside the state machine as configuration.
8. Wrapping the actual call, checking state before calling through
blocks.text: 8. Wrapping the actual call, checking state before calling through

blocks.content: The state machine alone does nothing. The important part is the wrapper function that every caller goes through instead of calling the downstream service directly.
The call wrapping logic
blocks.text: The call wrapping logic

blocks.content: Before attempting the real call, we ask the breaker if it is allowed. If not, we fail immediately or return a fallback. If yes, we make the call and report the outcome back to the breaker.
This wrapper is the only place callers interact with the breaker. The rest of your code just calls callThroughBreaker instead of calling the flaky service directly.
9. A worked example, wrapping a flaky service call
blocks.text: 9. A worked example, wrapping a flaky service call

blocks.content: Let us put it together with a fake service that fails on purpose for a while, then recovers, so we can watch the breaker trip and reset.
The flaky service
blocks.text: The flaky service

blocks.content: Imagine an inventory service that starts throwing errors for a stretch of calls, then goes back to responding normally.
Reading the trace
blocks.text: Reading the trace

blocks.content: Calls one and two succeed with the breaker Closed. Calls three, four and five fail, and after the third failure the threshold of three is crossed, so the breaker trips to Open.
Calls six and seven are rejected instantly by the breaker itself, without ever reaching the flaky service, even though the service was going to fail anyway at that point.

After call eight we sleep past the reset timeout. Call nine becomes the Half Open probe. Since the service has recovered by call nine, that probe succeeds and the breaker closes again, so call ten runs normally.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512287885-694325902.png
blocks.alt: Timeline diagram of the worked example showing calls one and two succeeding, calls three to five failing and tripping the breaker, calls six and seven rejected instantly, then the half open probe succeeding and normal calls resuming

blocks.title: What this buys you
blocks.text: During calls six and seven, real production traffic would have failed instantly instead of waiting on a timeout that was never going to succeed, which keeps the caller responsive and reduces load on the struggling service.

blocks.content: 10. Tuning thresholds and timeouts
blocks.text: 10. Tuning thresholds and timeouts

blocks.content: The pattern is simple, but picking good numbers for it takes some judgement based on the traffic and the downstream service.
Failure threshold
blocks.text: Failure threshold

blocks.content: Too low, and a couple of unlucky timeouts trip the breaker unnecessarily during normal blips. Too high, and you delay the fail fast benefit while the service is genuinely struggling.
Reset timeout
blocks.text: Reset timeout

blocks.content: Too short, and the breaker keeps flapping between Open and Half Open before the service has really recovered. Too long, and you keep rejecting calls well after the service is healthy again.
Failure rate over a fixed count
blocks.text: Failure rate over a fixed count

blocks.content: Many production implementations use a failure rate over a sliding window, for example fifty percent of the last twenty calls, rather than a raw count, since raw counts behave oddly under bursty traffic.

11. How Circuit Breaker fits alongside retries and timeouts
blocks.text: 11. How Circuit Breaker fits alongside retries and timeouts

blocks.content: Circuit Breaker is rarely used alone. It usually sits next to two other reliability patterns, timeouts and retries, and each one covers a different failure mode.
A timeout bounds how long a single call is allowed to take, so one slow request cannot hang forever. A retry handles the occasional, isolated failure by trying again, often with backoff.

Circuit Breaker steps in when failures stop being occasional and start being persistent. Retrying against a service that is completely down just multiplies the load on it, which is exactly the situation the breaker is built to prevent.

A common setup wraps the call with a timeout, wraps that with a retry for transient blips, and wraps the whole thing with a circuit breaker so that sustained failure stops the retries from hammering a service that needs time to recover.

blocks.title: Order matters
blocks.content: Put the circuit breaker on the outside. If it is Open, you want to skip the retries and the timeouts entirely, not run them uselessly against a service you already know is down.

Used together, these three patterns turn a single flaky dependency from a threat to your whole system into a contained, well understood failure that your service can shrug off and recover from on its own.
